FODS revision · reviewer comment 1(b)

A block resampling null for the change-point threshold

The reviewer says a quantile of the observed statistic is biased upward by the very changes we are looking for. Resampling fixes that — but only if the null preserves the dependence inside each metastable state.

Repo mfpy Results results/auto_block_null/ Companion block_permutation_null/FINDINGS.md Status works, with one open weakness

01 What the reviewer asked for

Threshold selection: using the quantile of the test statistic itself as the threshold is not appropriate in the multiple change point setting, as the presence of multiple change points will upwardly bias the quantile. This will be particularly apparent when the change sizes themselves are imbalanced: for example, if there are 2 (instantaneous) changes in the mean, and one is much larger than the other, the quantile-based threshold will be set too high to detect the smaller change. A simple work-around (whilst computationally more expensive), is to use a resample method; see e.g. Matteson and James 2014.

Reviewer report, major comment 1(b)

The objection is upward bias of the quantile under multiple changes, with a concrete consequence: small changes get missed when change sizes are imbalanced. Our own toy sweep confirmed the mechanism independently — the empirically optimal quantile tracks q* = 1 − (fraction of the series in transition), so the more of the trajectory that is elevated, the higher the cutoff climbs.

A resampling threshold answers this directly: calibrate the cutoff on data manufactured to contain no change, and it cannot be inflated by the changes present in the real series.

Untested The imbalanced-change-size case the reviewer offers as the sharp form of the argument has still not been run. It is the most direct evidence either way.

02 The construction

Let γ̇ₜ(w) be the windowed 2-Wasserstein statistic — the W₂ distance between the empirical measures of the left and right half-windows at t. The pipeline thresholds γ̇ at a cutoff c, takes maximal supra-threshold runs, and reads two change points out of each.

Three ways to set c:

  • Fixed quantile (incumbent) — c = Q_q(γ̇), a quantile of the observed statistic. This is what the reviewer objects to.
  • Permutation null (published) — shuffle all values, recompute γ̇, pool over R replicates and all t, take c = Q₀.₅(pooled).
  • Block bootstrap null (this work) — identical, but each replicate is built from contiguous blocks of length L rather than single points. L = 1 recovers the shuffle.

We use the circular scheme (Politis & Romano 1992): blocks are drawn from the series wrapped end to end, so every observation appears in exactly L candidate blocks and there is no edge deficit. The moving-block scheme (Künsch 1989) agrees to three decimal places on everything measured for L ≤ 400.

03 Why the full shuffle fails

A full shuffle is a valid "no change" null only if the process is iid within each state. That holds for the toy generator — independent Laplace draws inside each block — and fails for any SDE trajectory, where consecutive points inside a well are strongly correlated.

Destroy that correlation and the two half-window measures look far more alike than they ever do in the real data. The null statistic collapses, and the cutoff lands far too low.

04 Choosing the block length

L is bounded on both sides, and both bounds are physical:

  • Too short — within-state dependence is destroyed, the null collapses, and we are back to the shuffle failure.
  • Too long — blocks carry whole metastable states, so the replicate contains real change structure and stops being a no-change null. On the Langevin the cutoff falls again past L ≈ 200, and the segment count climbs back to 320 by L = 800.

So the target is: longer than the within-state correlation time, shorter than the dwell time. On the Langevin those are ~50–75 and ~1141.

The estimator, fully automatic

  1. Segment the series with the incumbent fixed-quantile rule at the manuscript's own (w, q). The pilot need not be good — only frequent enough that most segments lie inside one state, which is the fixed rule's behaviour, since its documented failure is over-cutting transitions rather than merging states.
  2. Trim w points from each segment end. Not a tuning knob: the pipeline's known boundary bias puts change points inside transitions, so both ends of every pilot segment carry ramp material — and a ramp is smooth, hence strongly autocorrelated. Untrimmed, the estimator returned τ_int up to 10 on toy data whose within-state process is iid, and on one case collapsed the whole trajectory into a single cluster.
  3. Estimate τ_int on each remaining interior by Sokal windowing; take the median.
  4. Set L = round(τ_int), build the block null, re-threshold.

 The Langevin row is the point of the section. Its whole-trajectory τ_int of 1676 is a metastability time, dominated by the well-to-well switching the method exists to detect. Any global stationary-series block-length selector returns that number, and it sits in the degenerate region. Segmenting first is what makes the estimate mean the right thing.

05 What it produces

Three rules, run end to end on each dataset with the manuscript's own (w, q) and no hand-set L anywhere.

Langevin — the incumbent's partition, recovered

RuleLSegmentskV₂ Cluster sizesfrac_core
Fixed quantile—15730.68548373 / 42051 / 95760.10 / 0.07 / 0.68
Full shuffle146620.62150060 / 499400.14 / 0.14
Automatic block5117230.68748997 / 41990 / 90130.10 / 0.07 / 0.69
 frac_core is the fraction of a cluster's points with |x| < 0.4 — between the wells — which is what identifies the transition state. The automatic block null recovers the incumbent's partition structurally, not merely score-equivalently: two wells of comparable size plus a transition cluster with the same core fraction. The full shuffle loses the transition state entirely and scatters its points into both wells.

Prinz — four wells, cleanly

The quadruple-well potential has minima at −0.739, −0.224, 0.269, 0.673. All three rules find them; the automatic block null and the shuffle return four wells plus one small transition cluster, while the fixed quantile additionally emits a degenerate 7-point cluster.

Toy — the control

The estimator returns L = 1 in every toy case, so the automatic rule reduces exactly to the published full shuffle there. That is the correct behaviour on iid-within-state data, and it is the check that the machinery does not invent dependence that is not present. Blocking with L > 1 on toy data actively hurts, monotonically — as a misspecified null should.

06 The open weakness

Block-join bias — read this before writing it up

The block null is not an unbiased "no change" null. Concatenating blocks drawn from unrelated parts of the trajectory creates an artificial discontinuity at every join, and a window of 2w = 430 points spans about eight joins at L = 51.

DistributionMeanMedian90th pctMax
Observed statistic0.3530.2690.7581.644
Full-shuffle null0.1220.1060.2060.561
Block null, L = 510.6810.6241.1452.173
 The block null's median sits above the observed statistic's 86th percentile.

So L ≈ 51 does not work because the null is correctly calibrated. It works because two errors of opposite sign cancel near the right cutoff — destroyed within-state dependence pushing the null down, block-join discontinuities pushing it up. That also explains the sharp sensitivity to L (k flips between L = 50 and L = 60), which a well-calibrated null would not show.

This has to be stated in the paper. A referee who knows the bootstrap literature will see it immediately. Two standard remedies exist and neither has been tried: the matched-block bootstrap (Carlstein et al. 1998), which chooses each successive block so its start is a plausible successor of the previous block's end, and the tapered block bootstrap (Paparoditis & Politis 2001), which down-weights block edges. The stationary bootstrap (Politis & Romano 1994) does not fix joins but removes the sensitivity to a single L, and is cheap to test.

07 Where this stands

Established The block null implemented and validated; L selected automatically with no per-dataset hand tuning; end-to-end clusterings on toy, Langevin and Prinz. On the Langevin it is parity with the incumbent, not improvement — the value is that the cutoff is calibrated on data containing no change, which is what answers 1(b).

Weakness The join bias above.

Open One w per dataset. The Langevin conclusion still rests on a single trajectory with a proxy ground truth. ADP's cluster count is near a boundary and its sensitivity to Z (fixed at 1.65) was never probed.

08 References

  1. Künsch, H. R. (1989). The jackknife and the bootstrap for general stationary observations. Annals of Statistics 17(3), 1217–1241. — origin of the moving-block bootstrap.
  2. Politis, D. N. & Romano, J. P. (1992). A circular block-resampling procedure for stationary data. In LePage & Billard (eds.), Exploring the Limits of Bootstrap, Wiley, 263–270. — the circular scheme used here.
  3. Politis, D. N. & Romano, J. P. (1994). The stationary bootstrap. JASA 89(428), 1303–1313. — random geometric block lengths; removes sensitivity to a single L.
  4. Carlstein, E., Do, K.-A., Hall, P., Hesterberg, T. & Künsch, H. R. (1998). Matched-block bootstrap for dependent data. Bernoulli 4(3), 305–328. — the standard fix for the join bias.
  5. Paparoditis, E. & Politis, D. N. (2001). Tapered block bootstrap. Biometrika 88(4), 1105–1119. — the other fix for the join bias.
  6. Politis, D. N. & White, H. (2004). Automatic block-length selection for the dependent bootstrap. Econometric Reviews 23(1), 53–70. Correction: Patton, Politis & White (2009), 28(4), 372–375. — the standard automatic selector. Not used here: it targets variance estimation for a sample mean under stationarity, and being global it would return the contaminated τ_int = 1676.
  7. Lahiri, S. N. (2003). Resampling Methods for Dependent Data. Springer. — textbook treatment of all of the above.
  8. Matteson, D. S. & James, N. A. (2014). A nonparametric approach for multiple change point analysis of multivariate data. JASA 109(505), 334–345. — the reviewer's citation. Methodology also in James & Matteson (2015), JSS 62(7), arXiv:1309.3295.
  9. Prinz, JH. et al. (2011). Markov models of molecular kinetics: generation and validation. J. Chem. Phys. 134(17), 174105. — the Prinz potential.

Verify page ranges against the publishers before these enter the .bib — volume, issue and year are confirmed; the ranges for Carlstein et al. and Politis & White come from secondary sources.
